engine_rules.name: Name 3-part stacked-fourth chords as sus4
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part stacked-fourth chord is labelled with cumbersome alterations (e.g., 'B Diminished triad [no b3rd] add b9') or C2 shorthand instead of the sus4 form.
engine_rules.anchor: My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4]. That means a G Major triad with 4 suspended for 3.

engine_rules.name: Name 4-part stacked-fourth chords as sus4
engine_rules.falsifier: A 4-part 4ths voicing is labelled as 'C Major 7th [no 5] substitute 4 for the missing 5th' rather than as a sus4 chord.
engine_rules.anchor: NAMES FOR 4-PART 4THS This is fairly simple: Sus 4 Chords...[I think it's the best way to go...]

engine_rules.name: Classify diatonic passages as event or episode by pitch-class content
engine_rules.falsifier: A passage is classified as event vs. episode based on its temporal length rather than the count of distinct diatonic notes it contains.
engine_rules.anchor: EVENT involves 2-6 diatonic scale notes at least once each. EPISODE involves all 7 diatonic scale notes at least once each.

engine_rules.name: Diatonically transposed events may collapse to intervallic identity
engine_rules.falsifier: Two diatonic transpositions of an event are treated as distinct sonorities when their interval structures are identical.
engine_rules.anchor: an event can be diatonically transposed to create 6 other events, but some of them will be intervallically identical.

engine_rules.name: Diatonically transposed episodes correspond to the seven modes
engine_rules.falsifier: An episode's transpositions are claimed to share the same mode rather than mapping one-to-one onto the seven diatonic modes.
engine_rules.anchor: an episode can be diatonically transposed to create 6 other episodes, where each corresponds to a different mode.

engine_rules.name: Name 3-part spread clusters by literal pitch content
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part spread cluster (e.g., the set C D E) is forced into a chord symbol like 'C Major 9 (no 5, no 7)' rather than written as 'C D E'.
engine_rules.anchor: Here’s what I think...Just name it like itis! CallitC DE"! [Daa!!!]

engine_rules.name: M-Lode pairs each 3-part family with exactly one 4-part counterpart
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part family is mapped to a 4-part counterpart outside of the five canonical pairings (e.g., triads paired with TBN I).
engine_rules.anchor: So, the REAL, COMPLEAT M-LODE depiction is: 3-Part Structures 4-Part Structures Triads (VolumelI) — 7th Chords 7th (no 3rd) TBNI 7th (no 5th) TBN IE 3-Part 4ths (Volume II) 4-Part 4ths 3-part Spread Clusters| Spread Clusters

engine_rules.name: Triad family interval content excludes 2nds and 7ths
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part chord containing a 2nd or a 7th between any voice pair is classified as a triad in the M-Lode sense.
engine_rules.anchor: The triads primarily consist of 3rds and 6ths with some 4ths and 5ths, but contain no 2nds or 7ths.

engine_rules.name: 3-part 4ths family interval content excludes 3rds and 6ths
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part chord containing a 3rd or a 6th between any voice pair is classified as a 3-part 4ths voicing.
engine_rules.anchor: While the 3-part 4ths primar- ily consist of 4ths and 5ths with some 2nds and 7ths, but contain no 3rds or 6ths.

engine_rules.name: Interval omission is restricted to triads, 3-part 4ths, and spread clusters
engine_rules.falsifier: Interval omission is treated as defining a member of the 7th-no-3rd, 7th-no-5th, TBN I, or TBN II family rather than as a structural property of triads / 3-part 4ths / spread clusters.
engine_rules.anchor: the omission of interval types only occurs within particular 3-part chord families (triad; 3-part 4th; spread cluster).

engine_rules.name: Prefer even-distribution families when crossing 3-part / 4-part density
engine_rules.falsifier: When the goal is consistent interval distribution across 3- and 4-part voicings, a non-even-distribution family (triad, 3-part 4ths, or spread cluster) is selected over the four even-distribution families.
engine_rules.anchor: the four chord families with the most even distribution are found both in 3- and 4-part chords (7th, no3rd; 7th, no5th; TBN I; TBN ID).

engine_rules.name: Derive 3-part voicings by omitting exactly one voice from a 4-part parent
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part voicing in the M-Lode framework is generated by omitting two voices, by adding a voice to a 2-part structure, or by any method other than single-voice omission from a 4-part parent.
engine_rules.anchor: What follows is a brief, introductory study of how to arrive at different 3-part chords by leaving out one voice of a 4-part chord.

engine_rules.name: A 4-part 7th chord generates the 7th-no-3rd and 7th-no-5th 3-part triads
engine_rules.falsifier: A 4-part 7th chord is claimed to derive a 3-part voicing other than 7th-no-3rd or 7th-no-5th by single-voice omission.
engine_rules.anchor: 7th chord generates _ two different triads, 7th (no 3rd), 7th (no 5th)

engine_rules.name: Each 3-part chord appears inside exactly four different 4-part families
engine_rules.falsifier: A 3-part chord is treated as embeddable in only one 4-part parent family, or in a number of parents other than four.
engine_rules.anchor: [Each 3-part chord appears four times...]

engine_rules.name: The chapter's five worked structures sit at positions 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 of the 35-structure taxonomy
engine_rules.falsifier: The five worked CMaj7 examples are claimed to exhaust the derivation taxonomy rather than to sample positions 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 of 35.
engine_rules.anchor: the five examples used in the present chapter (CMaj7, C, C, C, C ) correspond to numbers 1, 8, 15, 22 and 29. That means that there are only thirty more 4-part structures to explore in the present fashion!

engine_rules.name: Apply Drop 2 / Drop 3 / Drop 2&3 / Drop 2&4 / Double Drop 2 Drop 3 across TBN parents and inversions
engine_rules.falsifier: A TBN I or TBN II parent is derived to 3-part children using a procedure outside the named drop toolkit (e.g., random voice transposition) without justification.
engine_rules.anchor: 3-Part Chords Derived From a TBN I

engine_rules.name: Present material in C Major, expect transposition to melodic and harmonic minor
engine_rules.falsifier: Material is treated as valid only in C Major, with no expectation that the student extend it to melodic or harmonic minor.
engine_rules.anchor: All of the material that follows in this next section will be presented in C Major (no accidentals). The assumption is that our readers will have (by now) developed the necessary skills to make the needed adjustments to change the material to other 7-note scales.

engine_rules.name: Six generic A-B-C voice-leading patterns exist; explore the three alternates
engine_rules.falsifier: Voice-leading exploration is restricted to the three patterns used in Volumes I and II without ever considering the three new alternates.
engine_rules.anchor: Note: Only 3 different generic voice-leadings were used out of 6!

engine_rules.name: Use abstract A-B-C labels for chord-tone strands in generic VL formulas
engine_rules.falsifier: Generic voice-leading formulas are analyzed using scale-degree numbers rather than the abstract A/B/C strand labels, collapsing cycle independence.
engine_rules.anchor: Key: A= Ist note B = 2nd note C = 3rd note

engine_rules.name: Distinguish intervallic voice-leading from functional voice-leading via M.S.R.P.
engine_rules.falsifier: Voice-leading is described only by interval distance per voice, without identifying which voices form the M.S.R.P. cycle and which carry the chord-tone strands.
engine_rules.anchor: Functional Voice-Leading 1 7 3 5 Ascends 2 different voicing alternate (drop 3; drop 2 & 4) 2 voices are the cycle M.S.R.P.

engine_rules.name: Split 4-part voicings into top-2 / bottom-2 duets and add passing tones
engine_rules.falsifier: A 4-part voicing is elaborated by adding passing tones across all four voices simultaneously rather than via the top-2 / bottom-2 duet split.
engine_rules.anchor: 4-part; no passing tones Duet (top 2, bottom 2); add p.t.. ¢ NICE in Harmonic minor!

engine_rules.name: Twenty foundational 3-part chord types derive from Major, Melodic Minor, Harmonic Minor transposed to C
engine_rules.falsifier: The twenty foundational 3-part chord types are sourced from any scale outside Major / Melodic Minor / Harmonic Minor, or the close+spread inversion expansion is reported as a count other than 120.
engine_rules.anchor: All of the following 3-part chords are derived from the Major scale, the Melodic Minor and the Harmonic Minor scales, but they are transposed to the root of C. (Twenty 3-part chords is perhaps misleading...3 close inversions plus 3 spread inversions for each gives us one hundred twenty 3-part chords you should know...)

engine_rules.name: Prefer 3-part chords on guitar for playability and embellishment space
engine_rules.falsifier: On guitar, 4-part voicings are recommended over 3-part voicings without acknowledging the reduced embellishment space and increased fingering difficulty.
engine_rules.anchor: As guitarists, we can see that 3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords. Also, they often afford more space between the voices for melodic embellishment.

engine_rules.name: Use Grip-Slipping (Drop 3 in a six-tonic whole-tone system) to learn all inversions
engine_rules.falsifier: Grip-Slipping is presented as using a voicing type other than Drop 3 by default, or it omits the six-tonic / whole-tone organizing system.
engine_rules.anchor: "Grip-Slipping" is a term I use to describe a series of exercises that I sometimes give to my guitar students to help them learn all the inversions of different chords. Without giving away too many "secrets," I've included six examples incorporating seventh chords in a six tonic system (whole tone scale). The voicing type is Drop 3. (You might try Drop 2 and Drop 2 & 4 as well...)

engine_rules.name: Volumes I and II use GDVL; Grip-Slipping IVL/FVL examples are SCVL
engine_rules.falsifier: Volumes I and II are described as using SCVL, or Grip-Slipping IVL/FVL exercises are classified as GDVL.
engine_rules.anchor: P.S. The IVLs and the FVLs are all examples of SCVL (specific chromatic voice-leading), as opposed to GDVL (generic diatonic voice-leading), which is all of Volumes 1 & 2.

engine_rules.name: Convert C Major material to Harmonic Major by substituting Ab for A (b6)
engine_rules.falsifier: Conversion from C Major to Harmonic Major is performed by altering a degree other than the 6th (e.g., flatting the 3rd).
engine_rules.anchor: Harmonic Major...a major scale with b6...(sometimes named Ionian b6.) Ail of the “red pages” in Volumes 1 & 2 can be used with this very interesting variation: just play Ab (b6) instead of A (6).

engine_rules.name: Convert C Harmonic Minor material to Hungarian Minor by raising the 4th
engine_rules.falsifier: Conversion from Harmonic Minor to Hungarian Minor is performed without raising the 4th, or by altering a different degree.
engine_rules.anchor: Hungarian Minor...a harmonic minor scale with #4..|C D E}FEG AbBC |.

engine_rules.name: Present advanced M-Lode material across five parent scales
engine_rules.falsifier: Advanced M-Lode material is restricted to three scales (Major, Melodic Minor, Harmonic Minor) and never extended to Harmonic Major or Hungarian Minor.
engine_rules.anchor: We present it in 5 scales: 1. C Major 2. C Melodic Minor 3. C Harmonic Minor 4. C Harmonic Major (C Ionian b6) 5. C Hungarian Minor (C Harmonic Minor #4)

engine_rules.name: Voice-leading must treat melody and harmony as structural equals
engine_rules.anchor: I feel that excellent voice-leading treats both melody and harmony as equals.

engine_rules.name: Spread Clusters are the missing link that makes the M-Lode finite
engine_rules.falsifier: The 4-part chord taxonomy is treated as open-ended without recognizing 4-Part Spread Clusters as the closing family.
engine_rules.anchor: I had completely overlooked SPREAD CLUSTERS! I did some more musical math and real- ized that this was the missing link! It not only completed the set of 4-part chords, but it helped me to realize that this WORK was not only finite, but do-able!
